XX.1.title: The charge of the ancient kings
XX.1.reflection: The last book opens with words attributed to the sage kings: Yao charges Shun to hold to the mean, for if the people are in want, Heaven's gift will end; Tang takes the faults of the people on himself; Zhou rewards the good and restores what was lost. Food, mourning and sacrifice come first, and generosity, good faith, diligence and justice win the people. It reads as a collection of old charges, set here at the end as the inheritance Confucius claimed to pass on.
XX.1.question: What would you take on yourself, if you were responsible for others?

XX.2.title: Five excellent things, four bad
XX.2.reflection: Zizhang asks how to govern: honour five excellences and avoid four evils. Be generous without waste, demand labour without resentment, desire without greed, be at ease without pride, dignified without fierceness. The evils: to kill without having taught, which is cruelty; to demand results without warning, which is oppression; to be slow with orders and strict with deadlines, which is harm; and to be grudging in giving what is due, which is the manner of a petty clerk.
XX.2.question: Which of the four evils have you met at work, and which have you done?

XX.3.title: Knowing words, knowing people
XX.3.reflection: Without knowing Heaven's decree, one cannot be a junzi; without knowing ritual, one cannot stand; without knowing words, one cannot know people. The book ends on three kinds of knowing, and on words. The first book began with learning. Between them lie all the chapters, which is perhaps the point.
XX.3.question: Having come to the end, what word from the Analects will you keep?
XX.3.exercise: Choose one chapter you read in this cycle and read it again tomorrow.
